lead: Two AC waveforms can have the same peak but deliver different heating. Form factor and peak factor are ratios built from the RMS, average and peak values; they describe the shape of a waveform with plain numbers. Form factor is V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>avg</sub>; peak factor is V<sub>m</sub>/V<sub>rms</sub>. Meter scaling, rectifier design and insulation checks use them. For a sine wave the standard values are 1.11 and 1.414.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for peak, average and RMS values of a sine wave.

blocks.text: Three numbers describe a periodic voltage: peak V<sub>m</sub> (largest magnitude), RMS V<sub>rms</sub> (the DC voltage that gives the same heating), and average V<sub>avg</sub>. For a pure sine, the full-cycle average is zero because the positive and negative halves cancel. So we take the average of one half cycle, or of the rectified waveform. For a rectified wave, we take the average over a full cycle of the rectified shape. This choice matters: using zero makes the form factor infinite, which is meaningless.
F<sub>F</sub> = V<sub>rms</sub> / V<sub>avg</sub>,   F<sub>P</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> / V<sub>rms</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>m</sub> is peak voltage in volts (V); V<sub>rms</sub> is RMS voltage in volts (V); V<sub>avg</sub> is the average of the rectified voltage in volts (V). F<sub>F</sub> and F<sub>P</sub> are dimensionless.

blocks.text: The RMS value is the steady DC value that would produce the same power in a resistor. The average value is the area under the rectified curve divided by its base. Peak factor tells you how far the waveform reaches above its RMS; form factor tells you how much the RMS exceeds the average.

items: V<sub>m</sub> is peak voltage in volts (V).
V<sub>rms</sub> is RMS voltage in volts (V).
V<sub>avg</sub> is average of the rectified voltage in volts (V).
F<sub>F</sub> and F<sub>P</sub> are pure numbers, no units.

sections.h3: Values for sine and rectified sine

blocks.text: For a sine v = V<sub>m</sub> sin θ, the half-cycle average is V<sub>avg</sub> = (2/π)V<sub>m</sub> = 0.637 V<sub>m</sub>. The RMS is V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 V<sub>m</sub>. Then F<sub>F</sub> = 0.707/0.637 = π/(2√2) = 1.11. F<sub>P</sub> = 1/0.707 = √2 = 1.414.

A half-wave rectified sine keeps one half of each cycle. Its average over a full cycle is V<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.318 V<sub>m</sub>; its RMS is V<sub>m</sub>/2 = 0.5 V<sub>m</sub>. So F<sub>F</sub> = 0.5/0.318 = π/2 = 1.571 and F<sub>P</sub> = 2.00.

A full-wave rectified sine folds the negative half upward. The average is 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.637 V<sub>m</sub>; the RMS is still V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 V<sub>m</sub>. Its form and peak factors are the same as the sine: 1.11 and 1.414.

A square wave switches between +V<sub>m</sub> and −V<sub>m</sub>. Its rectified average is V<sub>m</sub> and its RMS is V<sub>m</sub>, so both factors are 1.00. A symmetrical triangular wave of peak V<sub>m</sub> has V<sub>avg</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/2 and V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√3, giving 1.15 and 1.73.

A moving-coil meter responds to average value, while a moving-iron meter responds to RMS. If a coil meter is calibrated to show RMS on a sine wave, it multiplies the average by 1.11. On a square wave that same meter reads about 11 % high, because the true form factor is 1.00. This is why the waveform shape must be known before trusting an AC meter. A true-RMS meter computes heating directly and avoids this error.

Peak factor sizes insulation and semiconductor ratings. A 230 V RMS sine has peak 230 × 1.414 = 325 V. A capacitor rated 250 V DC therefore cannot be used on this supply, because the peak exceeds its DC rating. An AC rating is an RMS rating, so a 250 V AC part is safe at 230 V RMS. Rectifier diodes in a capacitor-input filter must withstand the peak, not the RMS. In power quality, a high crest factor warns of pulse currents whose peaks stress components, so the equipment heats more than a resistor carrying the same RMS would.

examples.question: A full-wave rectified sine voltage has a peak value V<sub>m</sub> = 100 V. Find its average value, RMS value, form factor and peak factor.
steps: For a full-wave rectified sine, V<sub>avg</sub> = 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 2 × 100 V / 3.1416 = 63.66 V.
examples.answer: V<sub>avg</sub> = 63.7 V, V<sub>rms</sub> = 70.7 V, form factor = 1.11, peak factor = 1.41.
examples.check:
import math
Vm = 100
Vavg = 2*Vm/math.pi
Vrms = Vm/math.sqrt(2)
FF = Vrms/Vavg
PF = Vm/Vrms
print(f'{Vavg:.1f}')
print(f'{Vrms:.1f}')
print(f'{FF:.2f}')
print(f'{PF:.2f}')

traps: Full-cycle average of a pure sine is zero, not 0.637V<sub>m</sub>. Use the half-cycle average or the rectified average in the denominator.
Average value is not RMS value. For a sine, average is 0.637V<sub>m</sub>, RMS is 0.707V<sub>m</sub>; swapping them gives 0.90 instead of 1.11.
Form factor and peak factor have no unit. Writing 1.11 V is a unit slip.
Half-wave rectified sine has form factor 1.57 and peak factor 2.00. Do not copy the full-wave values 1.11 and 1.41.
For a square wave, RMS equals peak. The sine's V<sub>m</sub>/√2 does not apply.

quiz.q: Define form factor and peak factor, with their formulas.
quiz.a: Form factor = V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>avg</sub>; peak factor = V<sub>m</sub>/V<sub>rms</sub>. V<sub>avg</sub> is the average of the rectified waveform.

quiz.q: State the form factor and peak factor of a full-wave rectified sine.
Why is the average of a pure sine taken over a half cycle rather than a full cycle?
quiz.a: Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel and the average is zero. The half-cycle average gives 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.637V<sub>m</sub>, which is useful.

quiz.q: A half-wave rectified sine has peak 50 V. Find its average, RMS, form factor and peak factor.
quiz.a: V<sub>avg</sub> = 50/π = 15.9 V; V<sub>rms</sub> = 50/2 = 25 V; form factor = 25/15.9 = 1.57; peak factor = 50/25 = 2.00.

quiz.q: A sine wave has RMS value 230 V. Find its peak and half-cycle average.
An average-sensing meter calibrated for sine RMS reads 111 V on a square wave of peak 100 V. Explain the reading and state the true RMS.
quiz.a: The meter reads average × 1.11 = 100 × 1.11 = 111 V. True RMS of the square wave is 100 V, so the meter reads 11 % high.

quiz.q: Two waveforms have the same RMS 100 V but peak factors 1.41 and 2.00. Which needs higher insulation, and why?
quiz.a: Peak factor 2.00 gives peak 200 V versus 141 V, so it needs higher insulation. Peak factor converts RMS to peak.

beyond: Not for the exam. Crest factor appears in power quality standards and in LED driver design, where pulsed currents have high peaks but modest RMS. True-RMS multimeters compute RMS directly and do not rely on a fixed form factor, so they read distorted waveforms correctly. Search for crest factor power supply, true RMS versus average sensing, and rectifier ripple factor.
